{{Short description|British immunologist and zoologist (1925–2019)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
[[File:2012 6 June Leslie Baruch Brent 2.jpg|thumb|Leslie Baruch Brent, London 2012]]
'''Leslie Baruch Brent''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|MBE}} [[List of members of the European Academy of Sciences and Arts|MEASA]] (5 July 1925 – 21 December 2019) was a British [[immunology|immunologist]] and [[zoology|zoologist]]. He was [[Professor Emeritus]], [[University of London]], from 1990. An immunologist, he was the co-discoverer, with [[Peter Medawar]] and [[Rupert Billingham]], of [[Immune tolerance|acquired immunological tolerance]]. They injected cells from donor mice into fetal mice, and later neonatal mice, which would as adults receive donor skin grafts without rejection.

Brent was born Lothar Baruch, in Köslin, Germany (now [[Koszalin]], [[Poland]]), to German Jewish parents, Charlotte (Rosenthal) and Arthur Baruch.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Brent |first1=Baruch |title=Sunday's child? : A memoir |date=2009 |publisher=Bank House Books |location=New Romney (England) |isbn=978-1-904408-44-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Stolpersteine in Berlin |url=https://www.stolpersteine-berlin.de/en/biografie/4247 |website=www.stolpersteine-berlin.de |accessdate=29 August 2020}}</ref> To avoid persecution in the largely non-Jewish Köslin, his family placed him in the [[Jewish Orphanage Berlin-Pankow]] in Berlin in 1936. In 1938, at age 13, to escape the rising [[anti-Semitism]] of the [[Sturmabteilung]] (Storm Troopers) and teachers, Brent was sent to England on the first of the [[Kindertransport]]s and became a pupil at [[Anna Essinger]]'s [[Bunce Court School]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gerrie |first1=Anthea |title=Revealed: the wartime school that saved lives |url=https://www.thejc.com/lifestyle/lifestyle-features/53077/revealed-wartime-school-saved-lives |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111121045915/http://thejc.com/lifestyle/lifestyle-features/53077/revealed-wartime-school-saved-lives |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 November 2011 |website=[[The Jewish Chronicle]] |accessdate=29 August 2020 |date=11 August 2011}}</ref> His parents and older sister stayed behind in Germany.<ref name="lbb-bio">{{cite web |last1=Spier |first1=Howard |title=Leslie Baruch Brent: Ein Sonntagskind |url=http://ajr.org.uk/journalpdf/2004_november.pdf |website=AJR Journal |accessdate=29 August 2020 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425045318/http://ajr.org.uk/journalpdf/2004_november.pdf |archivedate=2012-04-25 |page=11 |date=November 2004}}</ref> Because his status as a German national would have made him liable to execution in the event of capture, he was advised to change his name. After the war, he found out that his parents were sent to [[Riga Ghetto|Riga]], Latvia, and executed. There are three [[stolpersteine]] for his parents and sister in Berlin.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brent |first1=Leslie Baruch |title=Building Bridges to Berlin |url=http://www.ajr.org.uk/journalpdf/2008_august.pdf |website=AJR Journal |accessdate=29 August 2020 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402072803/http://www.ajr.org.uk/journalpdf/2008_august.pdf |archivedate=2012-04-02 |page=15 |date=August 2008}}</ref> After the war, he became a British citizen and enrolled at [[University of Birmingham]] where he was president of the Guild of Undergraduates in 1950–1951. He received his Ph.D. at [[University College London]].

As a secular Jew who escaped [[the Holocaust]], Brent was highly critical of Israel's treatment of the Palestinians.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wohlan |first1=Margarethe |title=Viele Jahrzehnte wollten wir nicht über die Vergangenheit sprechen |url=https://www.deutschlandfunkkultur.de/viele-jahrzehnte-wollten-wir-nicht-ueber-die-vergangenheit.984.de.html?dram:article_id=153596 |website=Deutschlandfunk Kultur |accessdate=29 August 2020 |language=de-DE |date=11 September 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Brent |first1=Leslie |title=Editorial |url=http://jfjfp.com/?p=62391 |website=jfjfp.com |accessdate=29 August 2020 |date=15 July 2014}}</ref>

In 2012 he was interviewed and filmed for the documentary [[The Essential Link: The Story of Wilfrid Israel]] by [[Yonatan Nir]], in which he talked about his [[Kindertransport]] experience.

He was a member of the [[European Academy of Sciences and Arts]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.euro-acad.eu/members?utf8=%E2%9C%93&land=United+Kingdom&klass=&filter=&sort=&way=|title=Members - European Academy of Sciences and Arts|website=www.euro-acad.eu}}</ref> and an honorary member of the [[British Society for Immunology]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.immunology.org/about-us/our-people/our-members/honorary-members|title=Honorary members - British Society for Immunology|website=www.immunology.org}}</ref>

Brent died in December 2019, at the age of 94.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tributes to immunologist Leslie Brent, 94, who arrived on first Kindertransport |url=https://jewishnews.timesofisrael.com/tributes-to-immunologist-leslie-brent-94-who-arrived-on-first-kindertransport |website=jewishnews.timesofisrael.com |agency=Jewish News Reporter|accessdate=29 August 2020 |date=24 December 2019}}</ref> He was posthumously appointed [[Member of the Order of the British Empire]] (MBE) in the [[2020 New Year Honours]] for services to Holocaust education.<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=62866|supp=y|page=N16|date=28 December 2019}}</ref>

==Career==
* Laboratory technician, 1941–43
* Army service, 1943–47, Captain
* Lecturer, Department of [[Zoology]], UCL, 1954–1962
* Rockefeller Research Fellow, [[California Institute of Technology]], 1956–57
* Research scientist, [[National Institute for Medical Research]], 1962–65
* Professor of Zoology, [[University of Southampton]], 1965–69
* Professor of Immunology, St. Mary's Hospital Medical School, London, 1969–1990

==Other positions==
* European Editor, Transplantation, 1963–68
* Chairman: Wessex Branch, Institute of Biology, 1966–68
* General Secretary, British Transplantation Society, 1971–75
* President, The Transplantation Society, 1976–78
